data.title: MDQ Specification Audit: multiple-selection
data.scope: The `multiple-selection` question type: `docs/question-types/multiple-selection.md`, `schema/multiple-selection.yaml`, its grammar, and the shared specs it depends on (`docs/references/grammar.md`, `docs/references/patterns.md`, `docs/question-types/question-base.md`, `docs/exam.md`, `docs/responses.md`).

data.title: Contradictions
Ambiguities
Omissions
Inconsistencies
Grammar violations
Schema mismatches

data.methodology:
`scripts/spec_audit.py` passed all 14 steps before the audit (schema bundle, docs, corpus, Additional Rules tables, lint codes, frontmatter tables, schema agreement of mdq-py).

The lead auditor read the shared specs and `docs/question-types/multiple-selection.md` and recorded contradictions, ambiguities, omissions and inconsistencies.

One subagent turned the grammars of `docs/references/grammar.md` and of multiple selection into Lark grammars and tested them with accepted and rejected inputs derived from the stated rules.

An independent subagent reviewed the multiple-selection document against `schema/multiple-selection.yaml`, ran each complete example through `mdq validate`, and checked the Additional Rules table against the MUST, SHOULD and MAY statements of the text.

data.title: Type inference has no rule for a list of blank and unknown values
data.description: A list such as `* [ ] Manaus` / `* [?] Santos` matches none of the four rules: no value is `*`, a percentage, `x` or a letter, and not every value is blank. The spec does not say which type the list takes, so it does not say against which `value` rule `[?]` is checked. mdq-py reads it as multiple selection and reports `foreign-choice-marker` on `[?]`. The corpus only covers `[?]` next to an `[x]` (`examples/invalid/multiple-selection-unknown-marker.mdq.md`), where rule 2 applies.
data.impact: Two implementations can infer different types, or none, and report different codes for the same document.
data.fix: Relax rule 4 to 'no other rule applies: multiple selection' (what mdq-py does), and add an invalid example with only blank and unknown values.
data.conditions: A choice list without `type`, whose only values are blank and unknown markers.

data.title: Empty brackets `[]` in a choice list have no rule
data.snippet:
value : ws
      | ws? ("x" | "X") ws?
data.description: `value` needs at least one `ws`, so `* [] Santos` has no value. The spec does not say what such an item is: a foreign marker (`foreign-choice-marker`), an item that makes the list not a choice list (then a forbidden list in the stem, `forbidden-block-element`), or a `parse-error`. mdq-py and the corpus (`examples/invalid/multiple-choice-empty-brackets.mdq.md`) use `parse-error`, which no text of the spec states. There is no multiple-selection example.
data.impact: `[]` is a likely typo for `[ ]`. Implementations can disagree on the code, and one could read the list as prose and drop the question body.
data.fix: State in question-base.md, Type inference, that `[]` in a choice list is a `parse-error`, as mdq-py does, and add a multiple-selection invalid example.

data.title: Choices section does not say which parts of multiple-choice#choices apply
data.snippet:
Choices follow the same structure from [Multiple choice questions](multiple-choice.md#choices),
respecting the rules for the allowed `values` inside the initial square brackets.
data.description: The referenced section mixes shared rules (text, id, feedback, comment, AST mapping table, duplicate text, visual equivalence, derived ids) with rules that are only true for multiple choice: the `score` row of the AST table, 'A choice is correct when its score is 1', 'the student still picks a single choice', the score scale and the `many-correct-choices` lint. The sentence 'respecting the rules for the allowed values' excludes only the value rule. A reader must guess that `score` is replaced by `correct` and that the single-pick sentence does not apply.
data.impact: Readers and porters can apply multiple-choice-only rules (score derivation, single pick, many-correct-choices) to multiple selection.
data.fix: List the shared rules explicitly (text, id, feedback, comment, duplicates, visual equivalence, derived ids) and say that `correct` replaces the `score` row of the AST table; or move the shared choice rules to one shared section that both types reference.

data.title: Text never states the no-correct-choice and all-choices-correct lints
data.snippet:
| choices[].correct  | info     | no-correct-choice          | at least one choice should be correct                     |
| choices[].correct  | info     | all-choices-correct        | not every choice should be correct                        |
data.description: The Additional Rules table lists both info rules, but no sentence of multiple-selection.md states them with a MAY or explains why they matter. The text in multiple-choice.md about these codes refers to scores and to a single pick, so it does not carry over. For multiple selection the reason differs: with no correct choice, the empty response `{}` scores 1; with every choice correct, ticking all scores 1.
data.impact: The rule exists only in the table; the level and the rationale cannot be checked against the text.
data.fix: Add a sentence to Choices: 'Implementations MAY report, at the info level, a question with no correct choice (no-correct-choice) or with every choice correct (all-choices-correct)', with the reason above.

data.title: The T, F and _ notation of the grading table is not defined
data.description: The table writes markings with `T`, `F` and `_`, and expands `_` to `F`. The document says (line 140) that a student has no way to leave a choice unmarked, so a reader cannot tell what `F` is as opposed to `_`. The distinction only makes sense with responses.md, where `F` is an explicit `false` key and `_` is an absent key. The document does not say so.
data.impact: Readers can think that multiple selection has a third state, which the same document denies.
data.fix: Say before the table that `T` and `F` are the `true` and `false` values of the response mapping and `_` is an absent key (see responses.md#multiple-selection).

data.title: 'no way to explicitly leave it unmarked' reads as the opposite of its intent
data.snippet:
There
is no way to explicitly leave it unmarked. If that is necessary, prefer using
[true/false](true-false.md) questions.
data.description: Leaving a choice unmarked is exactly what an unticked checkbox does. The intended meaning is that a student cannot abstain on a choice: every choice gets a verdict. 'it' also has no clear referent (the choice? the question?).
data.impact: Minor confusion about the meaning of an unticked choice.
data.fix: Reword: 'A student cannot abstain on a single choice: an unticked choice is a false verdict. If abstention is needed, use true/false questions.'

data.title: 'When neither ... and outside an exam' joins two cases with 'and'
data.snippet:
When neither
the question nor the exam sets a strategy, and outside an exam, the strategy
is `"symmetric"`.
data.description: Read literally, the default applies only when both conditions hold: no strategy is set and the question is outside an exam. The intent (footnote [^1] and exam.md#inheritance) is either case. Inside an exam whose `grading` map lacks `multiple-selection`, exam.md also gives `symmetric`. The same sentence is in multiple-choice.md:229-231.
data.impact: Minor; the footnote settles it.
data.fix: Replace 'and outside an exam' with 'or the question is outside an exam' in both documents.

data.title: Body does not state the two-choice minimum, unlike multiple choice
data.snippet: Body consists of an unordered list of items. Each item follows the grammar:
data.description: multiple-choice.md:41 says 'an unordered list of at least two items'. multiple-selection.md states the minimum only in the Additional Rules table (schema `minItems: 2`).
data.impact: Minor inconsistency between parallel documents.
data.fix: Write 'an unordered list of at least two items'.

data.text: The grading table of multiple selection agrees with its formulas in every row, with exam.md#penalty (symmetric = 2 * partial - 1) and with the grading corpus.

Responses state the unticked-means-false rule, the equivalence of an absent key and `false`, and the difference between `null` (skipped) and `{}` (answered none), consistently with the Feedback and Grading sections.
The `grading` and `shuffle` inheritance of multiple selection uses the same wording, defaults and exam-map key as multiple choice and exam.md.

data.title: feedback_line and comment_line accept any indentation before the marker
data.snippet:
feedback_line : ws? ">" ws? md_inline* nl
comment_line  : ws? COMMENT_MARK ws? md_inline* nl
data.description: The prose (docs/references/grammar.md:117-121) allows at most three spaces of indentation before `>` or `!`, relative to the list item content, and says that with four or more the line is not a feedback or comment line. The leading `ws?` has no bound. Counter-example: the item `* [x] Rio` followed by the line `      > fb` (four spaces relative to the item content). Tested with Lark: the grammar parses the line as a `feedback_line`. Under CommonMark, the line is a paragraph continuation, so `> fb` is part of the choice text. The same applies to `!` lines and to a tab before the marker.
data.impact: A reader of the grammar alone gets a different choice text and feedback than the prose and CommonMark give. The Python implementation also reads the over-indented line as feedback, which suggests the grammar is what implementers follow.
data.fix: Bound the indentation in the rule (for example `INDENT: / {0,3}/`, with a note on how a tab counts), or state next to the snippet that `ws?` before a marker is limited by the Marker rule.
data.conditions: Feedback or comment line indented four or more columns relative to the item content.

data.title: lazy_line accepts feedback and comment lines, so the item grammar accepts two feedback blocks
data.snippet: lazy_line     : ws? md_inline+ nl
data.description: `md_inline` is any inline element, and a `>` or `!` character is inline text, so `lazy_line` matches a feedback line, a comment line, a list item or a heading. In the multiple-selection `item` rule (`md_inline* nl lazy_line* (blank_line* observations)?`), the lines of a first feedback block can then parse as lazy lines of the choice text. Counter-example, tested with Lark: `[ ] Nile` / `  > fb1` / blank line / `  > fb2` parses, with `> fb1` as choice text and `> fb2` as the feedback. `[ ] Nile` / `  > fb1` / `  ! c` / `  > fb2` also parses. The prose forbids both: a lazy line is a line without a marker (docs/references/grammar.md:127-131) and a second block of the same kind is a `parse-error` (docs/references/grammar.md:134-137, docs/question-types/multiple-selection.md:156). With a stub `lazy_line` that excludes lines starting with `>`, `!` (not `![`), list markers, `#` and fences, the grammar rejects both inputs as the prose requires.
data.impact: The grammar does not encode the one-block-of-each-kind rule that it appears to encode; the restriction exists only in prose.
data.fix: Make `lazy_line` exclude lines that start a feedback line, a comment line or a block that interrupts a paragraph, for example with a terminal that has a negative lookahead for these starts.
data.conditions: Item with a feedback or comment block.

data.title: No grammar defines which bracket contents count as a value, so `[]` has no defined outcome
data.snippet:
value : ws
      | ws? ("x" | "X") ws?
data.description: The `value` rule rejects `[]`, `[xx]`, `[ x x ]`, `[*]`, `[50%]`, `[v]` and `[U+00A0]` (tested with Lark). docs/question-types/question-base.md:217-222 says a value outside the `value` rule of the type is a `foreign-choice-marker`, and gives `[?]` as an example, but no grammar defines the generic bracket that counts as a value before the type is known. For `* [] Lima` in a list forced to multiple selection, the spec does not say whether the item is a foreign value (`foreign-choice-marker`), a `parse-error`, or a plain list item that makes the list not a choice list. The Python implementation reports `parse-error` for `[]` and `foreign-choice-marker` for `[xx]`.
data.impact: Implementations can report different codes, or infer a different body, for the same malformed marker.
data.fix: Declare a shared `any_value` rule (for example `"[" /[^\]\r\n]*/ "]"` at the start of the item) that type inference and `foreign-choice-marker` use, and state whether `[]` matches it.

data.title: The value bracket is read as a value when a link destination or reference follows it
data.snippet: item      : ws? "[" value "]" ws? (CHOICE_ID ws?)? md_inline* nl lazy_line* (blank_line* observations)?
data.description: `CHOICE_ID` has the lookahead `(?![(\[])` because a bracket followed by `(` or `[` starts a markdown link (docs/references/grammar.md:83-86). The value bracket has no such lookahead. Counter-examples, tested with Lark: `* [x](https://ibge.gov.br) Brasília` parses as a correct choice with the text `(https://ibge.gov.br) Brasília`, and `* [x][ref] Brasília` parses as a correct choice with the id `ref`. CommonMark reads `[x](https://ibge.gov.br)` as an inline link and `[x][ref]` as a full reference link when `ref` is defined. The Python implementation reads the first as a choice and the second as an epilogue paragraph (`forbidden-block-element`).
data.impact: Contrived input, but the grammar and the markdown layer disagree on whether the item is a choice.
data.fix: State that a value bracket followed by `(` or `[` is still the value (and the rest is text), or add the same lookahead to the value bracket and define the result.

data.title: The item rule accepts any indentation before the value
data.snippet: item      : ws? "[" value "]"
data.description: docs/references/grammar.md:54-57 says the source text is read at the start of a block and only spaces and tabs are accepted, but sets no limit. Counter-example, tested with Lark: `*      [x] Rio` (six spaces after the list marker) parses as a correct choice. Under CommonMark, five or more spaces after the marker make the item content an indented code block, so the item has no paragraph that starts with `[x]`. The feedback rules state a three-space limit; the item has none. The Python implementation accepts the input as a choice.
data.impact: The grammar accepts a choice that a markdown renderer shows as code.
data.fix: State the limit for the `ws?` before the value (CommonMark: at most four spaces after the list marker), or state that the grammar applies to the item content after CommonMark removes the marker and its padding.

data.title: No grammar defines the generic bracket that counts as a value for type inference and foreign-choice-marker
data.description: The `value` rule rejects `[]`, `[xx]`, `[ x x ]`, `[*]`, `[50%]`, `[v]` and `[U+00A0]` (tested with Lark). docs/question-types/question-base.md:217-222 says a value outside the `value` rule of the type is a `foreign-choice-marker`, and gives `[?]` as an example, and type inference reads "every item starts with `[value]`" before the type is known. No grammar defines that generic `[value]`: it is not stated whether `[xx]`, `[x x]`, `[Brasília]` or `[a b c]` at the start of an item is a foreign value (the list stays a choice list) or text (the list is not a choice list). The Python implementation reports `foreign-choice-marker` for `[xx]` and `[ x x ]`. The `[]` case is a special case of this gap (see F2).
data.fix: Declare a shared rule for the bracket at the start of a choice item (for example `"[" /[^\]\r\n]*/ "]"`, minus what CHOICE_ID or a link would take) that type inference and `foreign-choice-marker` use.

data.text: The multiple-selection `value` rule matches the stated markers exactly. Tested with Lark: it accepts `[ ]`, `[  ]`, `[\t]`, `[x]`, `[X]`, `[ x ]`, `[ X ]` and `[\tx\t]` (every form in examples/valid/multiple-selection/uppercase-x.mdq.md), and rejects `[*]`, `[?]`, `[50%]`, `[v]`, `[y]`, `[xx]`, `[ x x ]`, `[U+00A0]` and `[U+00A0x]`, which agrees with the `foreign-choice-marker` examples (examples/invalid/multiple-selection-forced-star.mdq.md, multiple-selection-unknown-marker.mdq.md) and with the rule that U+00A0 is text, not `ws`.

The CHOICE_ID token and its position in the item rule behave as the prose states. Tested with Lark: `[x] [amazonas] Amazonas` gives id `amazonas`; `[x] [brasilia]` gives id `brasilia` and empty text (the documented `blank-text` case); `[x] [IBGE](https://ibge.gov.br) site`, `[x] [amazonas][1] text` and the collapsed link `[x] [brasilia][]` give no id; `[x] [a b] text` and `[x] [-a] text` give no id because the content is not a SLUG.

With a stub `lazy_line` that excludes marker lines (see F10), the shared `observations` rules accept and reject what the prose states. Tested with Lark as the tail of the multiple-selection item: feedback only, comment only, feedback then comment, comment then feedback, a blank line between the text and the first block and between the two blocks, the grammar.md example with a lazy line and an empty `>` marker line, a `![img](x.png)` line as a lazy line of the feedback, and `! [IBGE](...)` as a comment are accepted. Two feedback blocks separated by a blank line, feedback-comment-feedback, two comment blocks, and a paragraph after the feedback are rejected.

The `nl` and `ws` rules hold for the multiple-selection item. Tested with Lark: items with LF, CRLF and CR line endings parse identically, and `ws` does not match U+00A0. A last line without a line ending is rejected by the grammar, which the prose covers by reading it as if it ended with `nl`.

data.title: Multiple selection does not state how a choice list is inferred as multiple selection
data.snippet:
Multiple selection questions are represented by an unordered list with an ASCII-art
rendition of a checkbox. The correct answers are marked with `[x]` and incorrect
ones are left blank.
data.description: multiple-choice.md:6-9 says when a list is inferred as multiple choice and links to type inference. multiple-selection.md says nothing: it does not state that a list with an `x`/`X` value, or a list whose values are all blank, is inferred as multiple selection (question-base.md:214-216), nor that a `*` or percentage value makes the list multiple choice instead. The all-blank case is used by examples/valid/multiple-selection/none-correct.mdq.md, which has no `type`.
data.impact: A reader of this page cannot tell that a list with no `[x]` is still multiple selection, or that one `[*]` turns the whole list into multiple choice.
data.fix: Add a sentence after the example that summarizes the inference rules for multiple selection and links to question-base.md#type-inference, as multiple-choice.md does.

data.title: Choices section imports the multiple-choice Choices section without saying which parts apply
data.snippet:
Choices follow the same structure as [Multiple choice questions](multiple-choice.md#choices),
respecting the rules for the allowed `values` inside the initial square brackets.
data.description: multiple-choice.md#choices mixes structural rules (feedback, comment, id, text normalization, duplicate text) with rules that are false for multiple selection: the `score` field and its range, 'A choice is correct when its score is 1', 'many-correct-choices', 'the student still picks a single choice', and 'An omitted value is treated differently depending on the grading parameter'. The reference does not say which parts apply. Only the `correct` field is redefined (lines 63-66). `values` also does not match the rule name `value`.
data.impact: A reader or implementer can carry multiple-choice semantics (score, single pick, many-correct-choices) into multiple selection.
data.fix: List the parts that apply (item layout, text, id, feedback and comment blocks, duplicate and visual-equivalence rules) and state that the score rules and the correct-count rules of multiple choice do not apply.

data.title: Zero and all-correct choice counts are only in the rules table
data.snippet:
| choices[].correct  | info     | no-correct-choice          | at least one choice should be correct                     |
| choices[].correct  | info     | all-choices-correct        | not every choice should be correct                        |
data.description: The prose of multiple-selection.md never says that a question with no correct choice, or with every choice correct, is valid, nor that an implementation MAY report it. The only prose source is multiple-choice.md:138-142, which defines these codes in terms of `score` (a choice is correct when its score is 1). The same applies to `duplicate-choice-text`, `duplicate-choice-id`, `missing-choice-id` and the one-block-of-each-kind `parse-error`: no sentence of this page states them; they come only through the indirect reference at line 60.
data.impact: The rules table carries requirements that the document text does not define for this type, so the level and the meaning of each rule rest on another type's prose.
data.fix: Add a paragraph to Choices: any number of choices MAY be correct, including none or all; implementations MAY report `no-correct-choice` and `all-choices-correct` at the info level. Restate or explicitly reference the duplicate and id rules.

data.title: Body omits the two-item minimum that multiple choice states
data.snippet: Body consists of an unordered list of items. Each item follows the grammar:
data.description: multiple-choice.md:41 says 'an unordered list of at least two items'. multiple-selection.md:39 has no minimum, although the rules table (line 147) and the schema (`minItems: 2`) require two choices.
data.impact: The Body section and the rules table disagree on first read.
data.fix: Write 'an unordered list of at least two items', as in multiple-choice.md.

data.title: Note says there is no way to leave a choice unmarked, which is what unticking is
data.snippet:
There
is no way to explicitly leave it unmarked. If that is necessary, prefer using
[true/false](true-false.md) questions.
data.description: The paragraph says the absence of a marking is false, then says there is no way to 'leave it unmarked'. Unticking a box is leaving it unmarked. The intended meaning is that the student cannot abstain on a choice (leave it unjudged), which is what true/false allows (responses.md, True/false).
data.impact: The sentence reads as self-contradictory.
data.fix: Write 'There is no way to abstain on a single choice. If that is necessary, use true/false questions.'

data.title: Grading table uses three marking states for a two-state question
data.description: The Markings column distinguishes `F` from `_` and the 'Expands to' column converts one to the other. In multiple selection a student can only tick or not tick (line 137-140, responses.md:61), so `F` and `_` are the same response. Rows 1-3 use `F` for 'not ticked' and rows 4-6 use `_` for the same thing.
data.impact: The table suggests that a student can mark a choice as false explicitly, which the type does not allow.
data.fix: Write the markings as ticked sets (`{1, 3}`, `{1}`, `{}`) or as `T`/`_` only, and drop the 'Expands to' column, or state that it only exists to show the convention.

data.title: Fallback rule for grading conflates two cases and omits the missing map key
data.snippet:
When neither
the question nor the exam sets a strategy, and outside an exam, the strategy
is `"symmetric"`.
data.description: 'When neither ... sets a strategy, and outside an exam' reads as one case with two conditions, but these are two separate cases (inside an exam that sets nothing, and outside an exam). It also does not cover an exam whose `grading` is a map without a `multiple-selection` key, which exam.md:347 resolves to `symmetric`.
data.impact: A reader can think the symmetric fallback only applies outside an exam.
data.fix: Write: 'The strategy is `"symmetric"` outside an exam, and in an exam that does not set one for multiple selection (no `grading`, or a map without a `multiple-selection` key).'

data.title: Rules table uses 'should' for info-level rules
data.snippet:
| choices[].text     | info     | visually-identical-choices | should not be visually equivalent to another choice[^2]   |
| choices[].correct  | info     | no-correct-choice          | at least one choice should be correct                     |
| choices[].correct  | info     | all-choices-correct        | not every choice should be correct                        |
| choices[].id       | info     | missing-choice-id          | should be defined in the document, instead of derived[^3] |
data.description: By the spec convention, SHOULD maps to `warning` and MAY to `info`. The source prose (multiple-choice.md:118, 140, 164) says implementations MAY report these cases, so the level is info, but the Rule column phrases them as 'should'. The same phrasing is in multiple-choice.md:288-292.
data.impact: A reader that maps the wording to a level gets `warning`, not `info`.
data.fix: Phrase the info rules as observations, for example 'is visually equivalent to another choice', 'no choice is correct', 'every choice is correct', 'has no id of its own'.

data.title: Rules table field for count rules is a choice field, but the code reports on the list
data.snippet: | choices[].correct  | info     | no-correct-choice          | at least one choice should be correct                     |
data.description: `no-correct-choice` and `all-choices-correct` are properties of the whole list. The Field column gives `choices[].correct`, but the corpus reports them at path `["choices"]` (examples/valid/multiple-selection/none-correct.lint.json, all-correct.lint.json).
data.impact: The Field column does not match the path that implementations report.
data.fix: Use `choices` in the Field column for both rows.

data.title: Schema grading description omits the per-type map of the exam
data.snippet:
`inherit`, the default, takes the exam's `grading` value, and
          is `symmetric` outside an exam.
data.description: multiple-selection.md:99-100 and exam.md (Grading) say that `inherit` takes the exam's `grading`, or its `multiple-selection` entry when it is a map, and that a missing key is `symmetric`. The schema description only mentions 'the exam's `grading` value', which is wrong when that value is a map.
data.impact: A reader of the schema alone cannot resolve `inherit` against a map-valued exam `grading`.
data.fix: Write: '`inherit`, the default, takes the exam's `grading` (its `multiple-selection` entry when it is a map, `symmetric` if the entry is missing), and is `symmetric` outside an exam.'

data.title: Schema top-level description lists only `choices` as an extension
data.snippet: Extends the common question-base schema with a `choices` field.
data.description: The schema also adds `grading` and `shuffle` (lines 23-44), which question-base.yaml does not declare, and which the Frontmatter table of multiple-selection.md lists.
data.impact: Minor: the description understates the fields of the type.
data.fix: Write 'with `choices`, `grading` and `shuffle` fields'.

data.title: No multiple-selection example has a second feedback or comment block, and mdq-py merges them
data.snippet: | choices[]          | error    | parse-error                | carries at most one feedback block and one comment block  |
data.description: grammar.md (One block of each kind) says a second block of the same kind is a `parse-error`, also when a blank line or a block of the other kind separates them. No example under examples/invalid/ exercises this for a multiple-selection choice (only ordering-two-feedback-blocks exists). mdq-py accepts both `> one` / blank line / `> three` and `> one` / `! c` / `> three` under one choice and joins the feedback into 'one three', with no error.
data.impact: The rule is not tested, and the reference implementation violates it without the suite noticing.
data.fix: Add invalid examples for a choice with two feedback blocks (separated by a blank line, and by a comment block), expecting `parse-error`.
data.conditions: mdq-py `mdq validate` on a choice with two `>` blocks.

data.title: Markdown-level blank-text and text-normalization cases are only covered by YAML examples
data.snippet:
In
`* [x] [brasilia]`, `brasilia` is the id and the text is empty, which is a
`blank-text` error.
data.description: The corpus has blank-text and duplicate-choice-text examples for multiple selection only in YAML (examples/invalid/model-only/multiple-selection-*.yaml). No `.mdq.md` example covers the `* [x] [brasilia]` case the spec gives, a choice with only feedback markers, two texts that differ only in whitespace, a multi-line (lazy line) choice text, or multi-line feedback. multiple-choice has `.mdq.md` examples for the blank-text cases.
data.impact: The parser path that produces these values for multiple selection is not tested.
data.fix: Add `.mdq.md` invalid examples for `* [x] [id]` with no text and for whitespace-only duplicate texts, and a valid example with multi-line choice text and feedback.

data.title: Grading corpus has no question with zero or all correct choices, or with two choices
data.snippet:
questions:
  # The table in multiple-selection.md, "Grading": answer key [T, F, T, F].
data.description: All grading cases have at least one correct and one incorrect choice. No case covers an answer key with no correct choice (where `ticks: []` scores 1 under every strategy) or with every choice correct, both of which the spec allows (rules at multiple-selection.md:158-159 are only info), nor the two-choice minimum.
data.impact: Edge cases of the grading formulas that the spec allows are not checked against implementations.
data.fix: Add grading cases with keys `{a: false, b: false}` and `{a: true, b: true}` for the three strategies.

data.text: The schema Choice requires `text` and `correct`, matching the REQUIRED `correct` in the spec, and its feedback description matches the wrongly-judged rule of the Feedback section.
The grading table values match examples/grading/multiple-selection.yaml for all three strategies, and exam.md Penalty quotes the same values.
The corpus covers uppercase and spaced `x` values, an all-blank list inferred without `type`, forced `[*]` and unknown `[?]` foreign markers, and every schema rule of the table.
The complete example document of the spec validates with mdq-py without errors or warnings.

data.snippet:
Choices follow the same structure as [Multiple choice questions](multiple-choice.md#choices),
respecting the rules for the allowed `values` inside the initial square brackets.

data.description: Read literally, the default applies only when both conditions hold: no strategy is set and the question is outside an exam. These are separate cases: an exam that sets nothing, and no exam. The sentence also does not cover an exam whose `grading` is a map without a `multiple-selection` key, which exam.md resolves to `symmetric`. The same sentence is in multiple-choice.md:229-231.
data.fix: Write: 'The strategy is `"symmetric"` outside an exam, and in an exam that does not set one for multiple selection (no `grading`, or a map without a `multiple-selection` key).' Apply the same wording in multiple-choice.md.

Add a paragraph to Choices: any number of choices MAY be correct, including none or all; implementations MAY report `no-correct-choice` and `all-choices-correct` at the info level, with the reason above.

Either write the markings as ticked sets (`{a, c}`, `{a}`, `{}`) and drop the 'Expands to' column, or say before the table that `T` and `F` are the `true` and `false` values of the response mapping and `_` is an absent key (see responses.md#multiple-selection). Recommended: ticked sets, since both forms are the same response.

data.text: The choice-item grammars leave to prose the rules that decide whether a line is a choice, a feedback line or text (indentation limits, lazy lines, the generic value bracket). mdq-py follows the looser grammar in several of these cases, so the prose is the only defense against drift between implementations.
multiple-selection.md imports multiple-choice.md#choices by reference. An edit to the multiple-choice text can change the rules of multiple selection without anyone reviewing that effect.

data.title: [Spec] Define the bracket at the start of a choice item
data.summary: The spec defines each type's `value` rule, but not the generic bracket that type inference and `foreign-choice-marker` read before the type is known. So `[]`, `[xx]`, a list of only blank and `[?]` values, and `[x](url)` have no stated result. Options: (a) declare one shared rule for the leading bracket in grammar.md, relax type inference rule 4 to 'no other rule applies: multiple selection', and state that `[]` is a `parse-error` (what mdq-py does); (b) treat any non-matching bracket as text, so the list is not a choice list. Recommended: (a), since it matches mdq-py and the corpus and never drops a body in silence.
acceptance: grammar.md declares the leading bracket rule used by type inference and foreign-choice-marker
question-base.md type inference covers a list of blank and unknown values
The spec states the code for `[]` and for a value bracket followed by `(` or `[`
Invalid examples cover `[]` and blank-plus-`[?]` in a multiple-selection list

data.title: [Spec] Make lazy_line exclude marker lines and test the one-block rule
data.summary: `lazy_line` matches `>` and `!` lines, so the item grammar accepts two feedback blocks, which the prose forbids; no multiple-selection example tests it, and mdq-py merges the blocks. Fix the terminal with a negative lookahead for marker and block-start lines, and add invalid examples.
acceptance: lazy_line in grammar.md rejects lines that start with `>`, `!` (not `![`), a list marker, `#` or a fence
Invalid multiple-selection examples with two feedback blocks (separated by a blank line, and by a comment) expect parse-error

data.title: [Spec] Bound the indentation in the choice item and feedback grammars
data.summary: `ws?` before the value and before `>`/`!` is unbounded, while the prose and CommonMark limit it. Options: (a) bound it in the rules; (b) state once in grammar.md that item grammars apply to the item content after CommonMark removes the list marker and its padding, and keep the three-space rule for markers. Recommended: (b), it keeps the snippets short and matches what markdown-it gives the implementations.
acceptance: grammar.md states how indentation before the value and the markers is bounded
A choice indented as code and a feedback line indented four columns have a stated result

data.title: [Spec] Make the multiple-selection Choices section self-contained
data.summary: Choices imports multiple-choice#choices without saying which parts apply, the info rules on the count of correct choices exist only in the table, and the page does not say when a list is inferred as multiple selection. Options: (a) list the shared parts and add the missing paragraphs to multiple-selection.md; (b) move the shared choice rules (text, id, feedback, comment, duplicates, visual equivalence, derived ids) to one shared section that multiple choice, multiple selection and true/false reference. Recommended: (b), it also removes the risk that an edit to multiple choice changes multiple selection.
acceptance: multiple-selection.md states which choice rules apply and that score rules do not
The text states no-correct-choice and all-choices-correct with MAY at the info level
multiple-selection.md summarizes its type inference and links to question-base.md#type-inference

data.title: [Spec] Clarify the grading table notation of multiple selection
data.summary: The table uses T, F and _ for a two-state question. Recommended: write markings as ticked sets and drop the 'Expands to' column.
acceptance: The grading table uses a notation the page defines
examples/grading/multiple-selection.yaml still agrees with the table

data.title: [Spec] Phrase info-level rules without 'should'
data.summary: The Rule column says 'should' for info rules, which by convention maps to warning. Rephrase them as observations in multiple-selection.md and multiple-choice.md.
acceptance: No info row of the two tables uses 'should' or 'must'

data.title: [Spec] Fill the multiple-selection corpus gaps
data.summary: Add `.mdq.md` examples for blank text, whitespace-only duplicate texts and multi-line text and feedback, and grading cases with no or all correct choices and with two choices.
acceptance: The new examples exist and spec_audit.py passes
Grading cases cover {a: false, b: false} and {a: true, b: true} under the three strategies

data.text: Define the leading bracket of a choice item and the type inference fallback, so every malformed marker has one stated result.
Tighten the shared item grammar: lazy lines without markers, and a stated indentation bound; add the matching invalid examples.
Make the Choices section of multiple selection self-contained, preferably by moving the shared choice rules to one section.
Apply the mechanical text and schema fixes in one pass.
